name: Mustard greens
summary: How Filipino farmers usually grow mustasa in the lowland cool months, sown straight in furrows or raised as seedlings and set out on beds, then picked for leaves or pulled whole. For small vegetable farms and backyard growers who sell it fresh or for burong mustasa.
season: Mustasa is a lowland favorite of the cooler months, best sown from about September to February, often on rice land after the wet season harvest. It can be grown in other months with water and some shade, but heat and heavy rain make it bolt or rot.
material: Seed, sown straight in furrows or in a seedbed or seedling tray. Farmers pick seed of a variety known to resist pests and diseases. Seedlings are ready to transplant after about four weeks, at three to four true leaves.
spacing: Furrows 15 to 25 cm apart with plants about 15 cm apart when sown straight. Transplanted seedlings 15 to 20 cm apart. One plant a hill.
water: Watered two to three times a week by hand, hose or furrow, more in dry weather. Rice land planted after the harvest still holds moisture for the first weeks.
fertilizer: Mostly organic: rotted chicken manure with carbonized rice hull mixed into the soil, plus weekly fermented plant juice or manure tea. Some farmers add a little urea after thinning.
care: Thinning direct sown rows, hand weeding, regular watering and a close eye on leaf eating insects. Onion or cosmos planted around the field is used by some growers to keep pests away.
harvest: Leaves are picked from about two to four weeks after transplanting, or about two months after direct sowing, while the stalks are crisp. Farmers pick outer leaves over several rounds or pull the whole plant, then wrap the bundles in banana leaves to keep them fresh. Much of it goes to burong mustasa.

steps.title: Plow twice
steps.how: Plow or dig the field two times so the soil is loose. Mustasa likes loose soil rich in organic matter, near water.

steps.title: Add manure and open furrows
steps.how: Mix rotted chicken manure and carbonized rice hull into the soil, about 1 kg of manure and 300 g of rice hull a square meter, then open furrows 15 to 25 cm apart.

steps.title: Sow in the furrows
steps.how: Drop the seed in the furrows about 15 cm apart and cover with a little soil, then water.

steps.title: Water two to three times a week
steps.how: Keep the soil moist, watering two to three times a week or more in dry spells.

steps.title: Thin and weed
steps.how: Pull extra seedlings where they crowd and pull the weeds so the plants get sun and food.

steps.title: Feed and scout
steps.how: Many growers water with fermented plant juice or manure tea once a week. Check under the leaves for aphids, caterpillars and diamondback moth larvae, and pull out plants with mottled, curled leaves.

steps.title: Wrap and keep fresh
steps.how: Wrap the bundles in banana leaves or plastic and keep them in the shade so they stay crisp.

steps.title: Pick the leaves or pull the plants
steps.how: From about two months after sowing, pick the outer leaves or pull whole plants while the stalks are still crisp and firm.

watering.traditional: Mustasa sown straight in the furrows is watered two to three times a week by hand, hose or furrow, more in dry spells. On rice land planted right after the wet season harvest, the soil still holds moisture for the first weeks and less watering is needed.
watering.method: Watering cans and hoses on small plots, furrows on bigger rice land fields. Water in the morning or late afternoon.
watering.rainfed: Sow on rice land right after the wet season harvest so the plants start on the moisture left in the soil, and water by can two to three times a week once it dries. Mulch with rice straw to hold moisture.
watering.dryseason: Water two to three times a week, more in hot, dry spells and on sandy soil. Water when the top soil is dry or the leaves droop by mid afternoon.
watering.wet: Heavy rain makes mustasa rot or bolt, so in the rainy months plant on raised beds with drainage and skip watering on wet days.

schedule.often: Water right after sowing, then every day or two until the seedlings are up
schedule.amount: A gentle watering that keeps the furrow damp
schedule.why: Shallow seed dies if the furrow dries before it comes up.

schedule.often: Two to three times a week, more often in dry spells. Water before thinning
schedule.amount: Enough to keep the soil moist to the roots
schedule.why: Young mustasa grows tender leaves only in moist soil.

schedule.often: Two to three times a week, or more if the leaves droop in the afternoon
schedule.why: Dry spells make the leaves small, tough and very hot, and push the plant to bolt.

schedule.often: Keep watering two to three times a week through the picking rounds
schedule.why: Crisp stalks and full leaves sell and pickle best.

critical: Leaf growth: dry spells give tough, bitter leaves and early bolting.

signs.dry: Leaves droop and stay small, the stalks turn tough and the plants send up flower stalks early.
signs.wet: Lower leaves yellow and rot at the base, and the plants go soft.

better: Mulch the furrows with rice straw to keep the soil moist between waterings.
Keep the watering regular so the leaves stay mild and the plants do not bolt.

ways.label: Seedlings set out on beds (lipat tanim)

steps.title: Sow in a seedbed or tray
steps.how: Fill a seedling tray or seedbed with a mix of carbonized rice hull, compost and vermicast, sow one seed a hole and water lightly. Keep in light shade.

steps.title: Prepare the beds
steps.how: Plow twice, mix in rotted chicken manure and carbonized rice hull, and form beds.

steps.title: Transplant in the cool hours
steps.how: When the seedlings are about four weeks old with three to four true leaves, set one seedling a hole 15 to 20 cm apart, in the morning or late afternoon, and water.

steps.title: Water and weed
steps.how: Water two to three times a week and pull weeds as they come.

steps.title: Scout for leaf eaters
steps.how: Check for aphids, caterpillars and diamondback moth larvae, and remove sick plants.

steps.title: Harvest the leaves
steps.how: Leaves are ready about two to four weeks after transplanting, while the stalks are crisp.

watering.traditional: Seedlings are raised in trays or a seedbed under light shade and watered lightly, then set out in the cool hours, watered right away and watered two to three times a week until the leaves are picked.
watering.method: Watering cans and hoses on small beds, furrows on bigger fields. Water in the morning or late afternoon.
watering.rainfed: Set the seedlings out on rice land right after the wet season harvest so they start on the moisture left in the soil, and mulch with rice straw. Water by can two to three times a week once the soil dries.
watering.dryseason: Water two to three times a week, more in hot, dry spells and on sandy soil. Water when the top soil is dry or the leaves droop by mid afternoon.
watering.wet: Use raised beds with drainage in the rainy months and skip watering on wet days. Heavy rain makes mustasa rot or bolt.

schedule.often: Water lightly every day or as the mix dries, under light shade
schedule.why: Seedlings rot at the base in soggy trays.

schedule.often: Water right after setting out in the morning or late afternoon, then daily until they stand up
schedule.amount: Soak the soil around each plant
schedule.why: The seedlings must root before the sun dries them.

schedule.often: Two to three times a week, more in dry spells. Water after weeding
schedule.why: Steady moisture gives big, mild, tender leaves.

schedule.often: Keep watering two to three times a week while picking
schedule.why: Well watered plants keep crisp after picking.

critical: Leaf growth: dry spells give tough, bitter leaves and early bolting.

signs.dry: Leaves droop and stay small, the stalks turn tough and the plants bolt early.
signs.wet: Lower leaves yellow and rot at the base, and the plants go soft.

better: Mulch the beds with rice straw to keep the soil moist between waterings.
A drip line or a fine hose head gives every plant the same water and saves time.

mistakes: Sowing in the hottest months, when mustasa bolts and turns tough and bitter.
Never thinning, so plants stay small and weak.
Letting the soil dry out, which makes the leaves hot and fibrous.
Growing mustasa after pechay, cabbage or radish on the same plot again and again.
Leaving sick, mottled plants in the field where insects spread the virus.
better: Use fresh seed of a pest and disease resistant variety and sow in the cool months.
Test the soil and add balanced fertilizer to the manure base by the result.
Thin on time and keep the moisture steady with mulch.
Rotate with crops outside the cabbage family and keep the field clean.
Scout twice a week and remove sick plants early.
